facts.text: Spironolactone is contraindicated in patients with hyperkalemia.
Spironolactone is contraindicated in patients with Addison’s disease.
Spironolactone is contraindicated when used concomitantly with eplerenone.
Hyperkalemia may occur; monitor serum potassium within 1 week of initiation or dose change and regularly thereafter, especially with renal impairment or potassium‑raising drugs.
Excessive diuresis can cause hypotension, dehydration, and worsening renal function; monitor volume status and renal function periodically.
facts.population: patients at risk of volume depletion

facts.text: Spironolactone can cause electrolyte disturbances (hyponatremia, hypomagnesemia, hypocalcemia, hypochloremic alkalosis) and hyperglycemia; monitor electrolytes, uric acid, and blood glucose periodically.
Gynecomastia may develop in ~9% of male heart‑failure patients on ~26 mg daily; risk increases with dose and duration, usually reversible after discontinuation.
Heart Failure: start 25 mg once daily if serum K⁺ ≤5.0 mEq/L and eGFR >50 mL/min/1.73 m²; may increase to 50 mg daily; reduce to every other day if hyperkalemia develops.
Heart Failure: if eGFR 30–50 mL/min/1.73 m², consider 25 mg every other day as initial dose.
Essential Hypertension: initiate 25–100 mg daily (single or divided doses); titrate at 2‑week intervals; doses >100 mg/day provide no additional BP benefit.
Edema: initiate in hospital, 100 mg daily (single or divided); may range 25–200 mg daily; when used as sole diuretic, give at least 5 days before dose increase.
Primary Hyperaldosteronism (pre‑surgery): 100–400 mg daily; for non‑surgical patients, use the lowest effective dose for maintenance.
Spironolactone tablets may be taken with or without food, but should be taken consistently with respect to meals.

Concomitant potassium supplements or potassium‑raising drugs (ACE inhibitors, ARBs, NSAIDs, heparin, TMP) increase risk of severe hyperkalemia; consider discontinuing potassium supplements and monitor serum K⁺.
Lithium clearance is reduced, raising lithium toxicity risk; monitor lithium levels periodically.
NSAIDs may blunt the diuretic, natriuretic, and antihypertensive effects of spironolactone; monitor clinical response when co‑administered.
Spironolactone interferes with digoxin radioimmunoassays, causing falsely elevated digoxin levels; use a non‑interfering assay.
Concurrent cholestyramine has been associated with hyperkalemic metabolic acidosis.
Aspirin may reduce spironolactone efficacy; dose titration and close observation may be required.
Elderly patients often have reduced renal function; monitor renal function closely when prescribing spironolactone.
Renal function should be monitored periodically; dose adjustments are recommended for eGFR <50 mL/min/1.73 m² (e.g., every‑other‑day dosing).
